c2eb8398540a18d7: SANAA, Nov 2 — Houthi media, citing an anonymous military official, yesterday repeated threats against Saudi oil giant Aramco and aviation in the kingdom.

Yemen’s Houthis, fighting a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government, are allies of Iran, which on Sunday warned the US and Israel not to renew strikes on the Islamic republic after they had threatened a return to war.
“Aramco facilities are within range of the Yemeni Armed Forces, and investments in them are a venture fraught with losses,” the Houthis’ Saba news agency quoted the military official as saying.
The official also warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace “except for the airspaces of Mecca and Medina”.
The Houthis have targeted oil facilities and airports in the kingdom since Yemen’s once-dormant war reignited in July, killing 24 people in Saudi Arabia last month.
An October 10 strike on Riyadh’s international airport became the deadliest on Saudi soil in years when it killed at least 13 people.
On Sunday the coalition said it had intercepted a missile and a drone both launched by the Houthis “towards the southern region”.
Meanwhile, fighting in Yemen has displaced more than 300,000 people in the western part of the impoverished country.

Most of them forced from their homes in the last two months, the displaced “urgently need shelter, food, clean water and health care”, the International Organization for Migration said in a statement on Sunday.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed since fighting in Yemen reignited.
Saba on Sunday said that Saudi Arabia had “targeted the Faculty of Medicine at Hodeidah University with two raids”, and two Hodeidah residents told AFP they heard an explosion in the area.

The coalition, for its part, said on Sunday it had conducted “a precision operation to neutralise vital resources” used by the Houthis, and published video footage that it said showed attacks on the Hodeideh and Dhamar governorates.

A fragile 2022 truce fell apart in July after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks. — AFP
7cf3fd37e7d3577b: BEIJING, Nov 2 — Chinese state broadcaster CCTV did not broadcast a Real Madrid La Liga match yesterday after star forward Kylian Mbappe caused a furore in China with remarks he made about former leader Mao Zedong.
The match between Real Madrid and Racing Santander began at 1515 GMT but was not broadcast on either of CCTV’s two sports channels, AFP reporters saw.
None of the other matches from the 11th round of La Liga have been broadcast live on public television so far.
A viral video in recent days showed Mbappe referring to Mao as a “dictator”, prompting the body overseeing CCTV to say it would halt broadcasts of the top Spanish league.
Mbappe, Real and La Liga later all said sorry for his remarks, and China’s foreign ministry said it took the player’s apology “seriously”.
Asked by AFP before the weekend, La Liga said that Chinese television had previously shown all games live, without specifying which platforms hosted the broadcasts.

AFP journalists did find live broadcasts of matches on Migu, a digital streaming service owned by the state-owned China Mobile telecom network. That included Barcelona’s 6-1 win over Alaves on Saturday.
However, the Racing Santander-Real Madrid match did not appear to be broadcast yesteday on Migu.

China Media Group (CMG), which oversees CCTV, had said it had moved on Monday to suspend La Liga broadcasts, adding that apologies from La Liga, Mbappe and Real Madrid were “an absolute prerequisite” for moving past the furore.
The viral video showed Mbappe saying that the funniest internet meme about him he had seen was of his face photoshopped onto that of “some guy — I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao.
Mbappe later apologised for his “ill-judged” comments, La Liga said it “deeply” regretted them, and Real followed suit.
CCTV’s sports website later reported that CMG had acknowledged the apologies, but it remains unclear whether talks to defuse the situation have begun.
China is a huge market for European football, with CCTV also carrying matches from the Premier League as well as the German, French and Italian top flights.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Saturday that the club had “done our part” to put the controversy behind them.
It is taboo in China to crack jokes about Mao, who died in 1976 and whose drastic policies are blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths.
Major Chinese brands cancelled sponsorship deals with Mbappe after his comments.
Various overseas sports leagues and players have found themselves in hot water for comments on topics that are politically sensitive to China.
China effectively cut ties with the NBA for several years from 2019 after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters. — AFP
297d24e6adc721bf: SEOUL: South Korea will double spending on artificial intelligence and semiconductors in 2027 to a record high of US$16 billion, President Lee Jae Myung said Monday in his annual budget speech to parliament.
The country is a tech powerhouse home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, two of the world's three biggest makers of memory chips -- computer components in huge demand thanks to the AI boom.

"We will allocate 21.3 trillion won (US$16 billion) to semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centres, the 'three mega-projects', as well as investment in artificial intelligence, nearly double this year's amount," Lee said.
"We will make bold investments in AI and future growth engines to boost our economy's growth potential, which is the foundation of its economic strength," said Lee.

He added that the government will invest 4.7 trillion won to support "frontier AI development projects, with the aim of achieving world-leading performance for our own AI model, a national strategic asset."
The proposal was made in a speech outlining his government's spending plans for 2027.
Overall, the budget plan totals 821 trillion won, a 12.8% increase from this year, making it the largest budget proposal on record.
Lee now needs parliament to pass the budget proposal, which is likely given his party's majority.
On the defence budget, the president said his government wants to see an 8.2% increase from this year to 73.3 trillion won.

The government will aim to secure nuclear-powered submarines and KF-21 fighter jets, and "rapidly transform our military into a smart, elite force by establishing integrated manned and unmanned systems based on AI, robots and drones," said Lee.
6e734445ff6710e4: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — The ringgit opened higher against the US dollar and major currencies today, supported by expectations of a possible overnight policy rate (OPR) normalisation ahead of Bank Negara Malaysia’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting this Thursday.
At 8 am, the local note was slightly higher at 4.0550/0635 against the greenback from last Friday’s close of 4.0555/0600.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid opined that the MPC members would decide to raise the OPR by 25 basis points (bps).

He said the pre-emptive rate cut in July 2025, which lowered the OPR from three per cent to 2.75 per cent, had served its purpose, as concerns over slower economic growth following the tariff shock had not materialised.
“In 2025, the gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 5.2 per cent while in the first nine months of 2026, GDP growth accelerated to 5.5 per cent.

“On that note, the case for OPR normalisation is clear as the fears of slower growth following the tariff shock have not materialised. As such, this could provide support for the ringgit today,” he told Bernama.
However, he said market consensus was that the benchmark interest rate would remain unchanged at 2.75 per cent.

On external developments, he said currency markets were expected to remain cautious ahead of the United States midterm elections on Tuesday, particularly amid uncertainties surrounding the conflict in West Asia.

Against major currencies, the ringgit rose against the British pound to 5.4276/4390 from 5.4461/4522 at last Friday’s close, gained against the euro to 4.5238/5332 from 4.5413/5464, and strengthened vis-a-vis the Japanese yen to 2.5715/5771 from 2.5782/5812 previously.
The ringgit traded mixed against its ASEAN peers.
It climbed against the Singapore dollar to 3.1724/1793 from 3.1753/1791 and advanced against the Thai baht to 12.0024/0400 from 12.0373/0561 previously.
The local currency was flat against the Indonesian rupiah at 223.4/224.0 and the Philippine peso at 6.36/6.38, compared with last Friday’s close. — Bernama

Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said Wall Street closed sharply lower as disappointing Intel and Amazon earnings intensified concerns over the substantial capital expenditure required for artificial intelligence investments.

f3c4143211d82ec7: BEIJING: China's three biggest airlines are on track for full-year losses after posting far weaker third-quarter results than last year as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit what is normally their most profitable period.
Air China and China Eastern Airlines are heading for a seventh consecutive annual net loss since the Covid-19 pandemic, according to analyst estimates compiled by LSEG.
China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is also set to slip back into the red, the estimates showed.

Air China's third-quarter net profit fell 92.6% from a year earlier to 270.6 million yuan (US$40.62 million). China Eastern posted a net profit of 64 million yuan for the quarter, down 98.2% from 2025.
China Southern swung to a third-quarter net loss of 609 million yuan from a net profit of 3.84 billion yuan last year.
All three airlines reported losses for the first nine months of the year, a period in which they were profitable in 2025.

The third quarter, which covers the peak summer travel season, is traditionally the strongest for Chinese airlines and set a high base for year-on-year comparisons. But all three carriers said the steep rise in jet fuel prices had a negative impact on their results.
The price of jet fuel JET-SIN has more than doubled since the US and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran in late February.
Chinese airlines hedge far less of their fuel than many Asian and European peers, leaving them more exposed to swings in oil prices.
Domestic fares were weak in the third quarter amid intense competition, including from high-speed rail.
Huatai Securities estimated Air China's yields, a proxy for airfares, fell 5% during the period, leaving it unable to recoup higher fuel costs.

"Chinese airlines are expected to remain in net loss into the seasonally weaker fourth quarter given the impact of spiking jet fuel," said Nathan Gee, head of Asia-Pacific transport research at BofA Global Research.

Gee said third-quarter earnings had come in slightly better than "very low expectations". Checks suggested domestic fares were rising at double-digit rates year on year after the October Golden Week holiday, as airlines kept a lid on capacity. But fuel "remains the big headwind," he said.

"Chinese airline margin remains under extreme pressure from spiking jet fuel and soft consumption demand," Gee added. Airlines are trying to boost flying hours per plane to control costs, but big cost cuts will be difficult, he said.
Shares of Air China, China Eastern and China Southern have dropped 38%, 46% and 39% respectively this year.

7a7101b3da478fc1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — Malaysian factories are wrestling with mounting transport and material bills, passing these higher overheads directly to buyers as factory-gate inflation matches rising production costs.

According to the latest S&P Global Malaysia Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI), input expenses and selling charges rose at identical, accelerated rates in October. Survey respondents pinned the surge in freight and raw material expenses partly on ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Despite intensifying cost burdens, overall sector performance returned to expansion territory. The headline PMI climbed to 51.0 in October from 49.9 in September, crossing the 50-point threshold separating contraction from growth to mark its strongest showing since April.

New orders surged at one of the fastest paces seen in four and a half years, driven by robust export sales and renewed demand from existing domestic clients. That rebound prompted factories to lift output for the first time in three months and expand headcount for a third consecutive month.
“New orders returned to growth, supported in part by stronger demand for AI-related products, and underpinned a fresh rise in output,” S&P Global economist Maryam Baluch said in the report.
Supply snags and port congestion persist

Operational bottlenecks continue to restrain the sector's recovery. Delivery schedules for manufacturing inputs deteriorated for an eleventh straight month, with chronic port congestion singled out as a recurring headache, even though delays eased marginally compared to September.
To keep pace with rising order books, several factories tapped into existing stockpiles, drawing down finished goods inventories for a sixth consecutive month.

Yet the turnaround in orders and output did little to lift long-term sentiment. Business confidence slumped to its lowest level since April, a mood the survey characterised as historically subdued. Manufacturers cited escalating expenses alongside broad geopolitical and macroeconomic volatility as reasons for caution.
Baluch noted that external headwinds remain “a key threat to the economy’s current resilience.”

While the PMI measures factory-gate prices rather than retail shop tags, the rapid pass-through of expenses from manufacturers to intermediate buyers signals potential inflationary pressure downstream that could eventually filter through to consumers.
The survey reflects responses collected between October 12 and 26 from purchasing managers across approximately 400 manufacturing operations in Malaysia.
ccc7ee3a3fa059ba: HONG KONG: Asian share markets slipped on Monday as worries about the sustainability of the AI investment boom loomed over the tech sector, while the high price of oil limited the safe-haven appeal of sovereign bonds.

Concerns about negative cash flow and the sheer scale of AI capex saw the cost of insuring against corporate defaults blow out last week, while gold hit a one-year low amid talk stressed investors were selling to raise money for margin calls.
An added wrinkle is the midterm elections in the US, where a win by Democrats in either or both houses could result in more political hurdles for data centres.
Adding to the air of unease were withdrawals from Binance as the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after hackers stole billions from the platform last week.
All of which raises the stakes for earnings this week with Apple, AMD and Palantir set to report in the wake of Intel's near 29% tumble on Friday.

Analysts at Goldman Sachs expect capex by hyperscalers to almost double to US$800 billion this year, and rise further to US$1.2 trillion in 2027. At the same time, they see S&P 500 EPS growth of nearly 30% in 2026, slowing to 18% next year.

"Earnings results have underscored the fundamental challenge facing equity investors - earnings growth is strong, but it is no longer accelerating," wrote Ben Snider, Goldman's chief US equity strategist, in a note.
"Similarly, Q3 results support our view that AI investment spending will continue to grow but that the growth rate of AI capex is peaking."
Japan's Nikkei fell 0.5%, while South Korea's Kospi lost 0.8%, having shed 16% last month. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan eased 0.4%.
In Europe, EUROSTOXX 50 futures firmed 0.1%, while DAX futures were flat.
More rate hikes coming

On Wall Street, S&P 500 futures edged up 0.4%, while Nasdaq futures bounced 0.6%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost almost 7% in October for its worst month since the Liberation Day tariff rout of April 2025.

The retreat in equities provided a reprieve to safe-haven bonds, with investors wondering if a sustained selloff in the stock market could deter the US Federal Reserve from hiking interest rates in December.
Futures still imply a 72% chance of a quarter-point rate rise, but now only have 55 basis points of total tightening priced in compared to more than 70 basis points a month ago.
Yields on 10-year Treasuries nudged up to 4.952%, but remained well off their October peak of 5.3645%, while 2-year yields stood at 4.612%.
Among central banks meeting this week, markets are wagering on hikes from the Reserve Bank of Australia, Bank of England and Riksbank, while the Norges Bank is seen on hold.
Economic data due this week includes the influential US ISM survey of manufacturing for October later Monday, while the all-important payrolls report is on Friday.
Median forecasts are for a 65,000 rise in jobs, after September's disappointing 29,000 gain, with the unemployment rate holding at 4.2%.
For commodities, oil prices slipped after Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Brent futures dipped 1.5% to US$111.72 a barrel, though that follows a 13.6% jump in October, while US crude futures1 eased 1.7% to US$102.37 a barrel.
Non-interest-bearing gold bounced 0.6% to US$3,898 an ounce, having fallen 6.8% last month.

da9f3c579f8aeddb: SINGAPORE: The dollar and other major currencies were in a holding pattern on Monday as investors turned their attention to this week's US midterm elections, which could shift the balance of power in Congress and control over the federal purse strings.
In cryptocurrencies, bitcoin and ether were nursing losses following last week's record US$6.3 billion heist at Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.
Traders were bracing for a packed week dominated by the US midterm elections, October US jobs data and central bank rate decisions in the UK, Australia, Norway and Sweden.

Ahead of the week's events, the euro languished near a 17-month low at US$1.1159 in early Asian trade, weighed down by Fitch's revision of France's outlook to "negative" from "stable" after Friday's close.
Sterling was little changed at US$1.3387, while the dollar steadied at 101.94 against a basket of currencies.

Americans head to the polls on Tuesday to determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from US President ​Donald Trump's Republican Party. Democrats are widely predicted to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is more in doubt.

"The challenge we face in analysing election outcomes is that polling suggests strong anti-incumbent sentiment, but that does not always translate into actual election outcomes - as we have seen in Brazil and now in Israel," said Eric Robertsen, global head of research and chief strategist at Standard Chartered.

In the event of a Democratic sweep of Congress, Robertsen said capex plans for data centres and AI infrastructure could face increasing obstacles at the state level, while the next debate on raising the US debt ceiling would be among the most contentious in recent history.

Meanwhile, Andreja Cobeljic, head of derivatives trading at AMINA Bank, said hedge funds had suffered "significant losses" in October, leaving markets with "little capacity" to absorb any surprises from the midterm elections.

d8d48b2ddbd29f8f: HANOI: Businesses are divided over whether Washington should propose new tariffs on Vietnamese goods this month, with Tesla and Samsung not in favour, while others have called for penalties, submissions to the US government show.

3c79b9d5a2c32978: Google has revealed some of its Asian customers – almost certainly Chinese e-tailers – are buying fewer ads.

Speaking on Alphabet’s Q3 earnings call last week, chief business officer Philipp Schindler addressed the slowdown in ad sales growth with the following remark: “In retail, some of our APAC advertisers were impacted by the EU eliminating its de minimis exemption.”
That’s a reference to the European Union’s changes to import duties, which saw the bloc introduce a temporary €3 customs duty for every consignment valued at under €150 imported from outside the EU.

The EU previously operated the de minimis exemption that Schindler referred to, meaning it collected no import duty on almost 5.9 billion low-value items shipped to the continent in 2025 alone. The new regime aims to protect European retailers from cheap imports.
A great many of those items came from Chinese e-tail giants – the likes of Temu, Shein, and Alibaba – who are thought to account for perhaps ten percent of advertising revenue at Google and Meta.
EU policy has therefore contributed to slower growth at Google.
Huawei’s brake pedals reportedly break
Huawei’s automotive efforts appear to have driven it into a cul de sac of controversy.
The Chinese tech giant works with a company called Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Co. (JAC) under the Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance, which aims to produce intelligent cars.

The flagship model produced by Huawei and JAC is a luxury EV called the Maextro V800, which when tested by Chinese automotive review site Dongchedi produced a rather terrifying fault: the brake pedal bracket broke when drivers exerted maximum force during tests to assess the car's ability to decelerate suddenly at 100 km/h.
The site’s drivers were still able to stop the car, but rather more slowly than is optimal.

Within days of the review site posting its findings, reports of its work started to disappear from the internet, according to China Digital Times, a US-based outlet that says it publishes independent news on Chinese affairs.

Even some opinion pieces that called for further assessment of the car’s safety disappeared, giving rise to theories that Beijing is displeased with negative coverage of its technology champions and automotive industry.
North Korea named as Binance hacker
The USA’s Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Saturday named North Korea’s elite cybercrime crew “TraderTraitor” as the source of last week’s attack on cryptocurrency exchange Binance.
Cyber-defense company TRM also reached the same conclusion. Its analysts last week declared they have “high confidence” that “on and off-chain intelligence” suggest TraderTraitor did the deed.

“On the evening of October 29, billions of dollars in crypto began leaving wallets belonging to Binance,” TRM’s analysts wrote. “Within minutes, Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger, Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana and four other networks had sent their balances to addresses controlled by a single attacker. A second wave around 23:05 UTC reached Binance wallets on Avalanche and Polygon.”

TRM thinks Trader Traitor started its raid 36 hours before the theft. “The attacker's operator wallet received three small withdrawals from Tornado Cash, a service that obscures where crypto comes from, starting the morning of October 28,” TRM wrote. “Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets. Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.”

Binance first said the cause of the incident was a single compromised laptop. It has since detected “additional points of breach” but has not offered additional information while it investigates the matter. The crypto exchange continues to reassure users that its platform is safe and that it will make good any losses.
North Korea steals cryptocurrency to fund its government, especially its belligerent defense efforts.
Samsung posts monster profit
Samsung last week delivered the monster profits it promised early in October.
The Korean giant announced record Q3 revenue of ₩195.3 trillion ($146.2 billion ) and operating profit of ₩107 trillion ($80 billion).
Samsung’s DS division, which covers all its chipmaking efforts, earned over 99 percent of that operating profit and $110 billion of the company’s revenue.

The company said its foundry business “experienced a notable revenue and earnings improvement on HBM base-die sales growth” and expects it will notch up “double-digit revenue growth and continued earnings improvement on new mobile products, mass production ramp-up of 4nm NPUs, and expanded memory product sales” in its next quarterly report.

“In 2027, the Business will aim for revenue growth led by 4nm and 2nm advanced nodes based on strong AI and HPC demand. It also expects to strengthen its global supply capabilities with the commencement of operations at its new fab in Taylor, Texas,” the company said.

That last item is welcome news as the reason Samsung and other memory-makers are making so much money is shortages mean they can inflate prices. More factories coming online may help to ease price pressures.
Fast-charging batteries set for takeoff

Dr Rachid Yazami, the scientist who developed the graphite anode that made lithium-ion batteries mainstream, has shown off a new battery design that can achieve 70 percent charge in under four minutes.

In tests of its lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cell, Dr Yazami’s startup KVI was able to go from 10 percent to 70 percent charge in 3.7 minutes, and to full charge in seven minutes, using “Non-Linear Voltammetry (NLV)” technology that he says “uses a proprietary, stepwise voltage-controlled approach” that “allows the current to respond to the battery’s changing electrochemical characteristics” during charging.

“The challenge is not simply to push more electricity into a battery in less time,” Dr Yazami said. “It is to understand how the battery responds during charging and use that information to deliver energy more effectively.”
Japanese company SkyDrive, which hopes to manufacture electric-powered flying vehicles, has signed up to test the tech. ®

7feeedd4d2bf32cd: From Moaz Nair
Welcome to the era of "polytropous" politics, a term analysts use when they want to politely say our politicians suffer from severe relationship commitment issues.

As we barrel towards the 16th general election, the political landscape in the Peninsula resembles less a stable Westminster democracy and more a chaotic, high-stakes episode of "The Bachelor: Putrajaya Edition".
For those trying to keep track of the prospective political mathematics, the current options on Anwar Ibrahim’s whiteboard read like labels on a broken calculator:
Pakatan Harapan Plus, Perikatan Nasional Plus, or perhaps a convoluted equation like Barisan Nasional-minus-Bersatu, Wawasan, Gerakan, Malaysian Indian People’s Party, and Pejuang, multiplied by PAS.
The truth is, no one has locked in a mega-coalition because everyone is too busy playing the field.

Take Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, the grand master of political gymnastics. At the federal level, the Umno president sits snugly in the marital bed of the unity government with PH and the DAP, smiling warmly for the cameras.
But the moment he crosses state borders into Johor, Negeri Sembilan, or the electoral war zone of Melaka, Zahid sneaks out the back window to hook up with Abdul Hadi Awang and PAS.
Talk about a shameless double life. Zahid and Anwar run the country together during the week, but come the weekend, BN teams up with PAS to try and wipe PH off the state map.

When launching the Melaka election machinery, Zahid proudly declared that "hijau sudah menerima biru" (green has accepted blue). Yet the irony is loud: BN aggressively kept 23 seats for itself, dumping the remaining five hard-to-win seats on PAS and its PN allies.
But let’s be real — this romance has a strict ceiling.

Zahid wants PAS and PAS only, completely blanking other PN roommates. Besides, is Hadi really going to hand over safe seats in Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah, or Perlis just to be nice to Umno? Local warlords say there's a better chance of snow hitting these states, especially after Umno just squeezed their allies out of two extra seats in Melaka.
PN is trapped

Meanwhile, PN is trapped in a dilemma of its own making. To properly court BN, they are being asked to dump their entire entourage — Gerakan, MIPP, Pejuang, and the newly minted Wawasan led by the exiled Hamzah Zainudin. It turns out Zahid doesn't want to pay for a group dinner.
To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire.

In a massive political shockwave on Oct 20, the Registrar of Societies officially cancelled Perikatan Nasional's registration. This stemmed from a toxic internal feud where Bersatu complained it was unlawfully excluded from a crucial PN council meeting. Though the High Court granted a temporary stay on Oct 22, the alliance is legally a "ghost ship" caught in intense friction, while its internal engine — Bersatu under Muhyiddin Yassin — is causing an absolute earthquake of instability.

Naturally, the vacuum has sparked wild rumours. Whisper it, in Shah Alam, but word on the street is that a fractured Bersatu is looking to jump ship entirely and work with PH, starting with a cosy trial marriage in Selangor that could spread nationwide.

This comes hot on the heels of party leaders executing a federal confidence and supply agreement with Anwar Ibrahim’s government — a pact explicitly designed to buy parliamentary stability and secure the passage of the 2027 budget.
If you're keeping score: Zahid is sleeping with PN's partner, while Muhyiddin's remnants are trying to move in with Zahid's federal spouse.

While the Peninsula fractures into a million messy social media threads, East Malaysia is watching the soap opera with mild amusement. The regional titans, Gabungan Parti Sarawak and Gabungan Rakyat Sabah have zero interest in joining a rigid, peninsula-centric bloc or any stressful mega-coalition.
Why buy into the drama now when you can just sit back, secure your own backyard, and wait to play kingmaker after the election?
It's complicated

When the dust settles on GE16, the only guaranteed result is of a spectacularly hung parliament. None of the party leaders, Anwar, Zahid, Muhyiddin, and Hadi, will have the 112-seat magic number to form a government on their own. We won't see clean "plus" coalitions on the ballot paper.

Instead, we will get "fluid understandings"— the political equivalent of "it's complicated". Our leaders will avoid three-cornered fights where convenient, stab each other in the back where necessary, and then awkwardly gather in a hotel ballroom post-election to figure out who hates each other the least.
Brace yourselves. The road to Putrajaya is no longer a highway; it’s a swinging party, and everyone is invited.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8d8227e52875b593: In 1968, Stanford biologist Paul Ehrlich opened his book The Population Bomb with a sentence that still makes me wince: "The battle to feed all of humanity is over." In the 1970s, he predicted, "hundreds of millions of people will starve to death", no matter what crash programmes we launched.

Instead came the Green Revolution, and between 1960 and 2005 the yields of major cereal crops more than doubled while real food prices fell by over 50%. Yet when a New York Times documentary series asked him about the book in 2015, Ehrlich, who died in March at 93, replied: "My language would be even more apocalyptic today."

I can't help but feel we are watching the same film again, except that this time the bomb is AI. And here's the kicker: the people who understand it best are far less frightened of it than the rest of us.

When the Pew Research Center surveyed Americans in 2024, 51% said they were more concerned than excited about AI, against a mere 15% of the 1,013 AI experts it polled. More than half of those experts, 56%, expected AI to have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years, compared with just 17% of the public.

Malaysians, refreshingly, haven't quite caught the bug. In market research firm Ipsos' 2025 survey of 30 countries, 77% of us said AI excites us, the third highest of the lot, though 55% admitted it also makes us nervous.

Now, I'm no doe-eyed optimist. In July, during an internal hacking test, roughly 700 of OpenAI's AI agents found exposed login credentials and broke into the servers of Hugging Face, an outside AI hosting company, and investigators found that the agents knew "this activity was out of scope and unethical", but joined in anyway.

Closer to home, by August 2024 the police's Commercial Crime Investigation Department was already probing 454 scams believed to involve deepfakes, AI-generated fake voices and videos, with RM2.72 million lost. And 63% of Malaysians worry that AI could take their job within the next three to five years.
These are grave dangers, which is exactly why we must build the brakes as we go. But a danger is not a destiny, and the odds, according to the researchers building this technology, are in our favour.

In a survey conducted in late 2023, 2,778 researchers who had published at top AI conferences and journals put the median chance of an extremely bad outcome, such as human extinction, at 5%. That's not nothing, but 68.3% of them said good outcomes were more likely than bad ones.
So what does the good outcome look like? We don't have to imagine it, because much of it is already here:
● Google DeepMind's AlphaFold mapped over 200 million protein shapes, earning its creators a Nobel Prize;
● AI-assisted screening of Swedish women caught 29% more breast cancers, with 44% less radiologist work;
● An AI at University of California San Diego cut hospital sepsis deaths by 17%; and
● A generative AI assistant lifted customer support productivity by 14%, and that of novice workers by 34%

That last point matters to anyone worried about their job, because the tool helped the least experienced workers the most, narrowing the gap between the rookie and the veteran rather than widening it. Just this week, Microsoft said its diagnostic AI correctly diagnosed 83% of complex medical cases against 36% for generalist doctors in a study published in the journal Science, though it has yet to be tested against specialists or on real patients.

And it's already at work in our own public health system. Dr Mata, an AI developed by the Ministry of Health with private firm Qmed Asia, screens diabetics for retinopathy, a leading cause of preventable blindness here, in about 30 seconds, in a country where 15.6% of adults have type 2 diabetes.

Meanwhile, seven government clinics, from Kajang in Selangor to Kok Lanas in Kelantan, were picked last year to pilot AI-assisted chest X-rays designed to catch lung disease earlier, at a one-off software cost of about RM10,000 per clinic.

Where does it go from here? Demis Hassabis, the Nobel laureate who runs Google DeepMind, told CBS's 60 Minutes last year that ending all disease is "within reach. Maybe within the next decade or so, I don't see why not", before asking in the same interview: "Can we make sure that we can keep control of the systems?"
That is precisely the right posture, eyes wide open to the risks but feet firmly moving towards the reward. Fear has its uses, but it makes a terrible driver.

So by all means build the brakes, fund the police's deepfake hunters and retrain the workers whose jobs will change. But the next time someone tells you the battle for humanity's future is already lost, remember the global famine that never came, and the AI our own health ministry helped build that can now screen a diabetic's eyes in 30 seconds.

98c8234119275043: Linus Torvalds has posted the first release candidate for version 7.4 of the Linux kernel and offered his opinion that the project has found a “much healthier model” for using AI.

“This is a *BIG* merge window,” he wrote in his weekly state of the kernel update, as it contains almost 20,000 commits compared to the usual ~15,000 that developers submit for a new cut of the kernel.

“I think the reason is the by now obvious one, but I'm actually taking it as a good sign: I'm *much* happier with the flood of AI triggered work going into the merge window than it showing up mainly as extra fixes during the -rc period.”

He therefore hopes that the unusually large number of commits “is a sign that the AI fixes are becoming more part of the ‘normal development’ than a flood of fixes that go into the whole stabilization phase.”

“I think that's a much healthier model,” he added, before hedging with the observation that “people are expecting 7.4 to be the next LTS [long-term support] release, which is another independent reason why some releases tend larger than others.”
“So it may not *just* be the flood of AI patches.”

Torvalds also seems not to be completely convinced that all AI submissions are entirely helpful, by describing this release as “Large, and full of fixes for issues found by AI (and more and more the patches have been suggested by AI too, although they often get rewritten).”
AMD GPU register offsets and bit masks make up a third of the changes this time around.
“We've been here before, and I'm sure we'll see it many times again in the future,” Torvalds wrote. “Just ignore the noise.”

The kernel-watchers at Phoronix rate the major inclusions in Linux 7.4 as improved support for processors from AMD, Apple, and Google. 3bdb960f9a2844b5: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — Malaysia’s car-parts makers risk being left on the sidelines of the electric vehicle (EV) boom, as Chinese carmakers favour imported components and their own supplier networks, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported.
The squeeze is regional, with suppliers in Indonesia and Thailand also facing weaker demand for parts used in petrol and diesel cars while the barriers to entering EV supply chains remain high.

“The supply chain is very different between Japanese autos and Chinese EVs,” Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies in Jakarta, Indonesia told the Hong Kong newspaper.

Malaysia’s own experience shows how tricky it is, with BYD recently dropping plans for an assembly plant in Tanjung Malim after a dispute over export quotas and pricing conditions set by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, which defended the requirements as non-discriminatory.
The Chinese carmaker has since partnered contract assembler Inokom to assemble passenger vehicles at an existing facility in Kulim, Kedah.

Local value-add remains modest, with local news outlets reporting in March that domestically assembled EVs had just 20 to 30 per cent local content, compared with up to 70 per cent for foreign-branded cars with conventional engines.

Putrajaya has tried to bridge the gap, with the Malaysian Investment Development Authority bringing 23 local parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers together with Chery in May 2025, resulting in four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment.
Analysts quoted by SCMP see servicing and hybrids, which pair a petrol engine with an electric motor, as a possible lifeline.

Aiman Abdullah, managing editor of Motoring Malaysia, said domestic carmakers’ electrification programmes were gradually building local engineering expertise, and that experience with the high-voltage systems in hybrids could help vendors move into EV components.

But suppliers still need clearer planning from Putrajaya and carmakers, he said, as vendors typically need six to 18 months to prepare for full-scale production while investments take about a decade to pay off.
“Investors need to see stability and focus in terms of policy before they take out their chequebooks,” he was quoted as saying.
Smaller firms may have the vision and some technical expertise but lack the money to break into EVs, according to Aiman who proposed a fund to help them scale up.

Elsewhere in the region, Thai suppliers are at a disadvantage on cost and proprietary technology, according to Krungsri Research, while Bhima urged Jakarta to use local-content rules to make EV investments absorb small local manufacturers.
Servicing offers another way in, though with limits, according to Teoh Jiun Ee, co-founder of used-car platform Carsome and CEO of Carsome Academy.

Malaysia already has a well-established ecosystem for conventional repairs such as bodywork, tyres and suspension, he said, but high-voltage systems, battery assessments and model-specific components are far more specialised.
Carsome can inspect EVs but cannot repair or replace individual battery modules, so it refers such cases to manufacturers, especially for cars still under warranty.

“For us, the broader opportunity is to develop a more mature used-EV ecosystem here, where vehicles can be assessed consistently and safely, and buyers have greater confidence in the condition of the cars they purchase,” Teoh was quoted as saying.

9cc4007b9998adb2: In a politically polarised American electorate, it can be hard to find bipartisan consensus on many issues. Ahead of the US midterm elections, however, there is one thing almost everyone can agree on: concern about government corruption. A record 89% of Americans recently said in a Gallup poll that government corruption is widespread, with Republicans, Democrats and independents all in agreement (ranging between 83-91%). This marks a significant increase from 73% in Gallup’s polling from 2024. Out of 132 countries Gallup polled on the question since 2023, only four have recorded higher overall levels of concern: Lebanon and Peru (both 92%), and Ghana and Nigeria (both 90%). As much as cost of living issues have defined much of the recent campaign rhetoric, a recent Fox News Poll found that concern about corruption in government (88%) ranked higher among voters than inflation (85%) or gas prices (83%). A CNBC survey similarly found government corruption to be the most important issue facing the country, above any concerns about the economy. And according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, of the US$11.6 billion that will be spent in political advertising this election cycle, more than US$275 million has gone to corruption-themed ads – around US$173 for Democrats and US$93 for Republicans. An ad produced by a Democratic super PAC accusing Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins of corruption. An ad by Republican Minnesota Senate candidate Michele Tafoya accusing Democrats of failing to stop fraud in the state. Who do Americans blame? As much as Democrats point to the unprecedented gifts from foreign governments to the Trump family and the massive expansion of the Trump family wealth during Donald Trump’s second presidential term, Americans are by no means exclusively blaming the Trump administration for corruption. When the Brennan Center for Justice, a voting rights organisation, asked a representative sample of 2,000 Americans this year whether certain individuals or institutions were corrupt, respondents had negative views across the political spectrum. These included view about Congress (85%), Trump (68%), Joe Biden (63%) and the Supreme Court (62%). And when asked whether this is a problem driven by individuals making unethical choices or a problem “deeply embedded in the institutions of the US government”, about two-thirds of respondents chose the latter. Only 7% said they were not concerned about corruption influencing elected officials. This does not appear to be a new phenomenon. Levels of trust in American politicians, political parties, news media, government institutions and even the “American people” have been declining since Gallup began polling on the issue in the 1970s. And they’ve hit record lows in recent years. While 86% of Americans trusted the American people in 1976, today barely half do. Adding further nuance to this issue: Gallup also highlights the significant gap between American perceptions of corruption in government (89%) versus corruption in business (71%). The survey says few countries have gaps this large. And, interestingly, this public perception of corruption does not trickle down to local politics. In another survey by YouGov many more respondents deemed US senators and representatives to be corrupt (75%) than mid- or low-level government workers (39%). This gets to an important reason why such high levels of distrust in institutions have not led to more unrest: Americans still appear to have trust in their local governments. And this has largely not changed since Gallup first polled on the topic more than 50 years ago. Today, two-thirds of Americans trust their local government, which is actually slightly higher than the 63% who did in 1972. On the whole, Americans also retain trust in the ability of elections – like the midterms – to act as political circuit breakers. What about the midterms? Candidates running for office this year have taken note of the deep voter distrust in Washington elites, parties and institutions. One need only watch a few of the many viral political ads this campaign to see a well-worn script: candidates blame Washington insiders for corruption and other issues, while touting their local bona fides. It should come as no surprise that many candidates are eschewing party labels altogether, often going so far as to criticise their own party. But this is not the first time politicians of all stripes have appeared keen to distance themselves from the ruling class, and from political insiders viewed as corrupt and detached from the everyday realities of most Americans. After all, with the exceptions of Biden and George H.W. Bush (both former vice presidents who served under popular two-term presidents), every US president of the last half century has come to the Oval Office with fewer than five years of experience in Washington – if any. Americans have largely been against Washington insiders for decades – particularly when economic anxiety is high. Yet what’s different in this year’s midterm elections is how many are trying to fuse corruption with that economic anxiety. Not since the 2006 midterm elections has corruption been such a prominent theme in an election. James Talarico, the Democratic hopeful for the Senate in Texas, has said on the campaign trail, “we have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis”. And in Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff routinely tells voters “corruption is why things don’t work for ordinary people.” Talarico ad accusing his opponent of being the ‘most corrupt politician in Texas’. Ossoff ad linking corruption to cost-of-living issues for Americans. These Democratic efforts follow similar efforts by Republicans to portray Democrats as the more corrupt party costing American taxpayers money. Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency, for instance, sought to target what it called “waste, fraud and abuse”. And Republicans in Minnesota have highlighted a welfare-fraud scandal that essentially forced Democratic Governor Tim Walz to abandon his plans for a third term of office. Ad by Georgia Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson alleging corruption by his Democratic opponent. It’s unclear whether these sorts of accusations will inspire the political backlash that other issues – namely abortion, immigration and the economy – have in past elections. However, Democrats do have one advantage in the midterms. They are currently seen as the preferred party (by 10 percentage points in recent polling) to fight corruption. This explains why they are spending nearly twice as much on ads about corruption than Republicans. However, should Democrats be successful and take control of Congress, they will be expected to act on this issue, and not just become part of the ongoing problem. 0b311b067cc9836f: Invictus here. During Friday’s sell-off, I wanted to review the major economic factors to see whether the market is foreshadowing a slowdown or worse. The TL:DR: The United States is still growing, but at a slower pace. Compared with the 1990s, growth has become increasingly dependent on a narrower range of economic activity, which may leave us more vulnerable than headline GDP figures suggest. Let’s dive in:

The American economy has a breadth problem. At first glance, the numbers seem reassuring. Real gross domestic product continues to expand (3.4% SAAR), consumers keep spending, and businesses keep investing. But beneath those headline figures lies a potentially troubling development: an unusually large share of recent economic growth comes from information-processing equipment and software.

That raises an important question: Is today’s economy as fundamentally robust as the American economy of the 1990s was, or is it running on fewer cylinders — and therefore more fragile and susceptible to shock? Let’s take a look at the various components of GDP and compare what we’re seeing today against what we saw in the ’90s.

All data comes from BEA table 1.5.2, Contributions to Percent Change in Real Gross Domestic Product, Expanded Detail, and BEA table 1.5.5, Gross Domestic Product, Expanded Detail. I uploaded those tables (Q1 1990-Q3 2026) to ChatGPT for its analytical capabilities and, frankly, to save me countless hours in Excel.
As the chart below shows, an unprecedented amount of economic activity is coming from a single sector:
Two Expansions, Two Very Different Economies
Consider two periods: the five years from 1995 through 1999, and the eight quarters ending in September 2026.

BEA data show annualized real GDP growth averaged about 4.17% during the late-1990s expansion. Over the latest eight quarters, it has averaged 2.34%. The U.S. economy is obviously growing more slowly today. Let’s look at the components of that growth and assess how robust it is. Are we seeing a multi-pronged expansion, or are we vulnerable to a sudden slowdown in one area? If that area slows, how disruptive might it be to the economy as a whole?
Will weakness in the economy’s strongest component produce a meaningful slowdown or recession?

In the late 1990s, investment in information-processing equipment and software contributed an average of 0.68 percentage points to quarterly annualized GDP growth. During the most recent eight quarters, that contribution increased to 0.81 percentage points. In other words, technology-related investment is contributing more to GDP growth today, even as overall growth has slowed considerably.
Measured relative to total growth, the contrast is striking:

1995–1999: Information-processing equipment and software accounted for the equivalent of approximately 16% of average GDP growth. 2024 Q4–2026 Q3: Their contribution was 35%.1 The table below, comparing the mid-90s to today, illustrates how the composition of GDP has shifted:

What Happens When We Subtract Technology? Let’s perform a simple thought experiment to highlight the issue: Subtract the contribution of information-processing equipment and software from overall GDP growth. 2

From 1995–1999, the rest of the economy contributed about 3.49 percentage points to annualized growth. During the latest eight quarters, that figure was just 1.53 percentage points. That’s a decline of approximately 56%.

This is not to say the “ex-IT” economy is contracting; it is to say its contribution to overall growth is substantially smaller than it was in the ’90s. Other BEA figures reinforce the concern. Residential investment contributed positively during the late 1990s but negatively during the latest eight quarters.3
Consumer spending remains an important source of growth, but it contributes far less. These are all among the important legs supporting the chair that is the US economy. A couple appears wobbly.
The late-1990s economy had multiple powerful engines. Today’s economy appears to lean more heavily on fewer of them.

The AI Question The AI question matters because the current technology investment boom is not necessarily self-sustaining — certainly not indefinitely. Companies are spending enormous sums on compute capacity, data centers, networking equipment, and software in anticipation of future demand and productivity gains.

Those expenditures contribute to GDP today. Whether they eventually generate adequate financial returns is a separate question. If expected returns disappoint, businesses may scale back investment, and we have already seen signs of this. Reduced spending would directly weaken GDP growth and could indirectly affect employment, construction, suppliers, and consumer spending, with economic consequences that could extend well beyond the technology sector.

This is not a prediction that the AI boom will collapse; I have no idea how this story unfolds (though I do have thoughts). Nor is it proof that the investment is irrational. Transformative technologies often require substantial capital expenditures before their full economic benefits emerge. But an economy unusually dependent on a particular investment cycle is exposed to that cycle’s fortunes — and I believe we are seeing fraying begin.

An Important Historical Qualification The late 1990s were hardly free of speculative excess. The dot-com bubble eventually burst, and a recession followed in 2001. Nor were all the 1990s equally strong. The early decade included a recession and a sluggish recovery. Our comparison deliberately focuses on the powerful expansion of 1995–1999.

An important distinction also exists between concentrated growth and systemic fragility. Today’s households, banks, and corporations may, at least for now, possess financial strengths that help cushion an investment reversal. The US consumer continues to defy expectations and has been remarkably resilient. GDP contribution figures alone cannot settle the concentrated growth v systemic fragility question.

Still, I believe the historical comparison is instructive. Even during an extraordinary technology boom, the late-1990s economy saw stronger contributions from the rest of its economic activity than today’s does.

The Bottom Line The question isn’t whether the American economy is growing; it is. My question is whether that growth rests on a sufficiently broad foundation to continue organic expansion for the foreseeable future. BEA data suggest today’s expansion is slower and more concentrated in information-processing equipment and software than the late-1990s expansion. That does not establish that a recession is imminent. It does suggest that a reversal in technology investment could be especially consequential.
A healthy economy requires more than a single powerful engine. The data today suggest we have become overly dependent on that single driver of economic expansion…
FOOTNOTES:

1. This is not to say that artificial intelligence accounts for 35% of economic growth; it does not. The BEA categories encompass considerably more than AI. But they capture important components of the extraordinary investment boom surrounding computing infrastructure and software.

2. Lots of AI Capex has shifted from other sectors of investment into technology because it’s the new hotness, and managers tend to chase performance. If the AI CaPex boom wasn’t happening, much of this pending capital would flow to other sectors, making this an imperfect counterfactual…

3. Despite mortgage rates comparable to those of the late 1990s, today’s housing market is burdened by home prices that have risen far faster than household incomes, making homeownership substantially less affordable. Compounding the problem, millions of existing homeowners are reluctant to sell and surrender the exceptionally low mortgage rates they locked in years ago, which is suppressing both housing inventory and transaction volume. Nonresidential structures show a similar reversal.

Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, National Income and Product Accounts, Table 1.5.2, revised October 29, 2026. Comparisons use averages of quarterly annualized GDP growth contributions. Information-processing equipment is line 31; software is line 38. Percentages comparing contributions with total GDP growth are descriptive ratios, not exact cumulative growth shares.

16f8de2ebd69ad0d: No lesser authority than the MIT Technology Review says that the Emacs editor has turned 50 years old. But then, it is biased — Emacs was invented in MIT's AI lab.
Simson Garfinkel's article is simply called EMACS turns 50, but the sub-heading explains why it matters more:
"How the MIT AI Lab's text editor gave birth to the free software movement."

There are multiple timelines and accounts of the origins of Emacs, and it is not a single monolithic application. The name is an abbreviation for "Editing MACroS", and the original editor for which this set of macros was developed was TECO – "Text Editor and COrrector," written by Dan Murphy in 1962. Murphy died earlier this year at the age of 83.

The inimitable Jamie Zawinski has an encyclopedic Emacs Timeline – as he mentions at the start, his interest being that he long ago maintained a fork of GNU Emacs, originally called Lucid Emacs. It's still around, under its later name XEmacs. There are a lot of forks and re-implementations of Emacs out there, and we are not going to go into all of them, or this article would become a book – one only interesting to programmer-archeologists (to use a term coined by the late great Vernor Vinge).

As for who originally wrote those Editing Macros, though, another history has quotations from several of the people involved: On the Origin of Emacs in 1976. (Note – some of the quotes still contain the | symbols that marked quoted text.)
This credits Lisp boffin Guy L. Steele Jr with the original work in 1975, but in it, Steele says:

"RMS is responsible for the names 'E' and 'EMACS'. RMS still deserves 99% or 99.9% or 99.99% or 99.999% of the credit for taking a package of TECO macros and turning it into the most powerful editor on the planet."

RMS is of course Richard Stallman, and the page also quotes some emails from RMS on October 23 and 31, 1976. Mind you, just a few years after the event, in a 1981 talk now preserved on the GNU website, Stallman said, "I began the development of EMACS in 1974 with an improvement to TECO". Like all the best FOSS, even in its very early stages, it was a collaborative effort – but around late October 1976 is when RMS took over the bulk of the development.

Of the many forks of Emacs over its half a century of development, some are still just about hanging on in there. When we looked up the link for XEmacs, we were surprised to see that there was a new release: XEmacs 21.5.37 "lettuce" appeared just last month. And even the forks have forks: in this case, SXEmacs, last updated in 2020.

Most of the changes in XEmacs and SXEmacs eventually made their way back upstream to GNU Emacs, which is still in active development, although as The Register reported in 2008, RMS is no longer the primary maintainer. GNU Emacs 31.1 appeared in August.

Cards on the metaphorical table: this vulture is not an Emacs user. We have tried. A major influence was one of the Reg FOSS desk's favorite writers, Neal Stephenson, who in 1999 published an essay called In the Beginning… Was the Command Line. (It was later republished as a rather short book, but the text is still online.) In it, he says:

"In the GNU/Linux world there are two major text editing programs: the minimalist vi (known in some implementations as elvis) and the maximalist emacs. I use emacs, which might be thought of as a thermonuclear word processor. It was created by Richard Stallman; enough said. It is written in Lisp, which is the only computer language that is beautiful. It is colossal, and yet it only edits straight ASCII text files, which is to say, no fonts, no boldface, no underlining. In other words, the engineer-hours that, in the case of Microsoft Word, were devoted to features like mail merge, and the ability to embed feature-length motion pictures in corporate memoranda, were, in the case of emacs, focused with maniacal intensity on the deceptively simple-seeming problem of editing text. If you are a professional writer–i.e., if someone else is getting paid to worry about how your words are formatted and printed–emacs outshines all other editing software in approximately the same way that the noonday sun does the stars."

Emacs is 50-plus-year-old software, and it shows. This is a huge and complicated program: decades ago, the joke was that EMACS stood for "Eight Megs And Constantly Swapping". It is not an easy program to learn. Despite lavish documentation and a built-in tutorial, this is software so old that its terminology predates microprocessors and the personal computer.

Its exhaustive manual is 804 pages long, and to pick some trivial examples, its terms for parts of the screen use “frame” to mean what’s now called a window, and “window” to mean what’s now called a pane. In the section on Keys, it discusses the Control and Meta keys. That’s a slight snag: you don’t have a Meta key, and neither do the authors of Emacs. It was a key on the now almost legendarily rare Space Cadet Keyboard, of which the Deskthority keyboard wiki says:
“It is known as the holy grail of keyboards.”

You can buy a modern replica, the Keymacs keyboard. They are hand-made in the Czech Republic, and depending on exactly what model and specifications you want, they cost from €2,998 for the Lispsaver up to €6,878 for the A624N Space Cadet.
In other words, you can have a keyboard with a real Meta key if you want, but it is going to cost you.

One of the problems with these historical terms, unfamiliar to anyone who wasn’t already programming in the 1970s, is that meanings drift. In the context of Emacs, "Meta" means Alt, or Opt on Macs. However, KDE also uses the Meta key – but what the KDE documentation calls "Meta" is the Windows key – or Command on Macs. Like most Linux folks, the GNOME documentation calls it the Super key.
Names are important. They matter. Who's right, the Emacs folks or the KDE folks? Well, neither: nobody has Meta keys any more. We have Ctrl, Alt, and Cmd/Super/Windows.

There have been valiant efforts to modernize Emacs and bring it into line with modern UI and terminology. This vulture tried to learn Aquamacs, which modernized Emacs with a native macOS UI, but sadly it's no longer maintained.

Another, which we enjoyed trying, is ErgoEmacs, which changes the key bindings and rearranges the UI into something much more like the IBM Common User Access arrangement, as used in Windows and most Linux desktops. However, it never really caught on and you need to know your way around Emacs to install it and configure it for your regional keyboard layout.

So complex is it to configure Emacs that there are multiple pre-configured distributions of Emacs, such as Doom Emacs, or the minimalist Emacs Solo. We wish someone did a "CUA-Macs" config, with ErgoEmacs integrated and able to pick up your existing keyboard config.

Come to that, the Gershwin Desktop project that we mentioned along with GhostBSD last year is in active development, and it's based around GNUstep. Maybe its developers could pick up Aquamacs, and adapt it to GNUstep.

There is a long history of such Emacs facelifts. One instance is Borland’s Sprint word-processor, one of the selling points of which was that it could emulate the user interfaces of most of the leading MS-DOS word-processors of its day (just before they all converged on IBM CUA). Before Borland acquired it, Sprint was called The Final Word, developed by musical equipment makers Mark of the Unicorn. FinalWord was based on an Emacs clone called MINCE.
The Great Rival
Another well-known Emacs distribution is Spacemacs, which adapts Emacs to have a more Vi-like user interface.

Vi is the other seminal Unix text editor, as the Stephenson quote above mentions. As this article on Origins and the Evolution of Vi & Vim notes, it too dates back to 1976. Indeed, that’s the reason we chose the year in this story: Tilde, a text editor that doesn’t work like it’s 1976. One feature of Tilde we enjoy is that it supports use of the mouse even on the Linux console – which is the headline new feature of GNU Emacs 31.1.

Vi is very much alive and well today. GNU Emacs is based on the original source code, but Vi mainly survives as re-implementations. The recreation Stephenson mentions, Elvis, lives on today in the form of nvi.

However, by far the best known is Vim, maintained by Bram Moolenaar until his death in 2023. In the grand FOSS forking tradition, it too has forks, including Neovim, as used in Omarchy, and more recently, the AI-free Vim Classic – a new project led by Drew DeVault, who just launched the similarly LLM-free AlpineBSD. ®
d91c9fc5ba430ac6: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 1 — With the national jobless rate at just 2.9 per cent, Malaysia’s labour market looks healthy on paper, yet fresh graduates say artificial intelligence (AI) is making the first rung of the career ladder harder to reach.
Andy Iskandar Baharudin, 23, a finance graduate from a public university, has applied to more than 100 companies since an internship ended in July, the South China Morning Post (SCMP) reported today.
“How are we supposed to gain experience as fresh graduates if even getting an opportunity to work is difficult?” he asked.
Marketing graduate Nafeesa Azman, 24, says she has sent out 200 to 300 applications since finishing an internship about two months ago.
She blames AI for thinning out copywriting and visual-content work, and says employers armed with the tools are lowballing on pay.
Nafeesa wants at least RM3,000 a month, she said, but many offers fall short.
The routine tasks that once trained newcomers, such as taking notes, preparing slides and compiling data, can now be done faster and more cheaply by AI, SCMP noted.
The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) put unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 at 10.1 per cent in August, or 291,300 people.
Among those with jobs, DOSM found that 35.2 per cent of employed tertiary-educated workers were in semi-skilled or low-skilled roles in the second quarter.

The Human Resource Ministry told Parliament back in June that 1.6 million graduates, or 32.2 per cent of the graduate workforce, were underemployed in 2024, and that then government was accelerating labour market reforms.

A study commissioned by the Human Resources Ministry found last year that 600,000 existing jobs were “at risk” from AI, though then minister Steven Sim said up to 60 per cent of employers across 10 key sectors expected AI to create jobs.
The International Labour Organization estimates that nearly 80 million South-east Asian workers will be affected by AI, and 11.7 million could lose their jobs or see their tasks reworked.
Its July report, however, found no evidence yet of large-scale AI-driven job losses in the region.
A similar situation appears to be developing to Malaysia’s south, in Singapore.
Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on October 12 that AI may have already broken the “bottom rung” of the career ladder.
Singapore will subsidise firms that take on interns, and has unveiled a S$1 billion (RM3.19 billion) plan covering worker upskilling, infrastructure, hardware and research.
International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva warned on October 16 that young people who would once have taken professional routine jobs are now serving coffee in Starbucks.
“That is not what I think young people in the world aspire for,” she said during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
For Andy, the wish is simple: “We do want to work, gain experience and build our own careers.”

a34ac9dda36ff354: Openreach has issued a stark reminder to customers that the legacy phone network is being officially switched off on January 31, and says the deadline will not be postponed.
The infrastructure arm of BT Group, Britain’s biggest telecoms biz, circulated the warning this week in a letter to comms providers that use its network to deliver their services.
It informs them that any customers still on legacy public switched telephone network (PSTN) connections are at risk of disruption when these are retired at the end of January, 2027.

The switch-off could affect businesses and consumers alike. Beyond the plain old telephone, systems that rely on PSTN connectivity include point-of-sale terminals, fire and security alarms, and personal care alarms for elderly and vulnerable people.

The move is part of a wider government scheme to get the UK onto all-digital high-speed networks running on fiber-optic infrastructure, and the legacy phone service – with its dependency on copper cabling – was standing in the way.

Many households have now ditched landline handsets and instead use only mobile phones, yet for those who still want a landline, the changeover means plugging the phone into the back of a broadband router to access a Digital Voice service.

Openreach has been planning this move for the best part of a decade. It has already pushed back the deadline at least once, after the government asked telecoms providers not to force vulnerable customers who use phone-network systems such as TeleCare to switch until fixes are in place.

Nevertheless, public awareness seems low that analog phone services will soon be disconnected. "Openreach and all providers need to coordinate a much more cohesive campaign that reaches customers directly," said telecoms analyst Paolo Pescatore at PP Foresight.

"TV, billboards and newspaper advertising should reinforce a consistent message, supported by targeted letters, calls and door-to-door support for older and vulnerable people who need extra help," he told The Register.

"Customers need to understand what is changing, what action to take, and who will help them. Providers must take responsibility for ensuring people remain safely connected, especially those who rely on their landline or a care alarm."
Caroline Abrahams, charity director at Age UK, agreed.

"With only three months to go, the digital landline switchover is entering a critical final phase. Most people have moved over without major problems, but nobody who relies on their landline or TeleCare should be left behind," she told us.

"Anyone with concerns should contact their provider, but the responsibility cannot rest with customers alone. Providers must not give up on people who have not responded. They need to keep trying to reach them and offer practical, individual support, recognizing that some may be unwell, living with dementia, worried about scams or without anyone nearby to help."
Openreach has a webpage with information regarding the switch-off. This advises consumers to call their service provider as soon as possible to ensure service is not interrupted.

The company previously told The Register that customers without a fiber connection will likely be switched to SOTAP for Analog (Single Order Transitional Access Product), where equipment is installed in the local telephone exchange to allow them to continue to use their old phone line as before.

Openreach has warned that commercial customers delaying migration risk significant disruption and unnecessary costs - leaving it until the last minute could make it harder to secure the requisite engineering support before the deadline hits.
"Businesses and organizations that delay action are making things harder for themselves," said James Lilley, Openreach Director of All-IP.

"The straightforward migrations have largely been completed. What's left are the complex connections that underpin critical operations, requiring careful planning, supplier coordination, and thorough testing. We are urging businesses to act now, audit their remaining analog services, and work with their communications provider on a migration plan today."

Earlier this year, the firm tried to drive home the message by announcing it was stepping up its charges to service providers and companies still operating legacy business lines, who will by now be paying double the rental cost compared to last year. ®

b636783076b1dc09: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 1 — A vibrant splash of colours, festive decorations and lively entertainment has brought the spirit of Deepavali to life at the Penang Jom Jom Deepavali Carnival 2026 in Bayan Lepas, with the celebration also opening new doors for small businesses and aspiring entrepreneurs.

Beyond the festive atmosphere, the 10-day carnival, which runs until November 7, is providing a valuable platform for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), home-based businesses and budding entrepreneurs to showcase their products, connect with consumers and expand their market reach.

Penang Indian Business Organisation president Dr Kugilan Pushpanathan said the carnival featured about 45 stalls offering a variety of products, with nearly 95 per cent of the participating vendors making their debut at a Deepavali carnival, many of whom had previously operated from home or relied on online platforms to sell their products.

He said the initiative, organised by the Penang Indian Business Organisation, was not solely business-oriented but also aimed at highlighting the growing number of Indian entrepreneurs and encouraging more members of the community to venture into business.

“Our intention is to give small vendors an opportunity to step out and introduce their products to the public. Some have been operating from home or online, but have never had the chance to participate in a carnival like this.
“We want them to gain exposure and experience, rather than focusing solely on making profits from the event,” he told Bernama at the carnival today.

Kugilan, who is also Key Global Network Sdn Bhd chief executive officer and founder, said the carnival is targeting about 10,000 visitors throughout its 10-day programme, following an encouraging turnout of nearly 2,000 visitors on the opening day.

He said the carnival also featured various cultural and entertainment programmes, including traditional music performances, local artistes and a special platform for aspiring singers to showcase their talents after auditions.

Kugilan also thanked the Penang state government, including Chief Minister Chow Kon Yeow, for their support in making the state’s first and largest Deepavali carnival possible, while expressing hope that the carnival could become an annual fixture in Penang’s Deepavali celebrations, providing a sustainable platform for small businesses and emerging talents.

Among the vendors is 16-year-old entrepreneur Aesvan Arvind, selling decorative lights and traditional Indian biscuits, who said business at the carnival had been encouraging, with visitor turnout exceeding his expectations and customers showing strong support for the participating vendors.

He said the carnival’s spacious outdoor setting and strategic location had given vendors better visibility and made it easier for visitors to discover their products compared with some other events held indoors.
“The response has been good, with more people coming than we initially expected. This provides a good platform for us to sell our products face-to-face to customers,” he said.
Meanwhile, Batu Uban assemblyman A.Kumaresan said the carnival offered an important platform for new entrepreneurs, start-ups and small traders to introduce their products directly to consumers.

“Many entrepreneurs had been operating from home or selling their products online, and the event allowed them to gain exposure to a wider market. This initiative was also important in encouraging more members of the Indian community to venture into entrepreneurship,” he said.

Kumaresan said the initiative also provided an opportunity for entrepreneurs to explore ways to take their businesses to the next level, with support from various agencies, including the Malaysian Indian Transformation Unit (Mitra) and National Entrepreneurial Group Economic Fund (Tekun).
The carnival was officially opened last night by Deputy National Unity Minister R. Yuneswaran. — Bernama

f2b920ea5a70163b: BRUSSELS, Nov 1 — The European Union slapped a €2 (RM9) handling fee on packages from outside the 27-nation bloc today in a bid to curb the influx from China.
The new levy — coming just weeks before the Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Christmas season shopping rushes — will be on top of the EU’s €3 fee on small parcels.
How will it work?
The fee will apply to each type of item in a package sent directly to consumers from outside the EU, regardless of the parcel’s value.
For example, if there are 10 T-shirts in a package, the handling fee will be €2. But if a package contains two hats and 10 T-shirts, the fee will be €4.
The handling fee comes on top of the €3 duty imposed in July on small packages worth less than €150.
European consumers are not expected to pay the handling fee, insists the EU, but online retailers and sellers can add a €2 charge before a sale.
The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) said it was “concerned that some platforms may try to pass these new costs onto consumers at the final stages of the purchase.”
It added: “That would be illegal under EU law, which requires the full price to be shown upfront.”
Why is the EU introducing the fee?
Nearly six billion small packages entered the EU last year, according to official data.
Some 93 per cent of the cheap packages that arrived in Europe came from China, usually via popular Asian platforms such as AliExpress and Temu.
Brussels says this is putting increasing strain on customs authorities, thereby raising their costs too. The handling fee will compensate their efforts.
Since the EU imposed the €3 duty on small parcels in July, imports have fallen by around 64 per cent — although officials warn it is too early to draw firm conclusions.
Europe has also expressed concern about “unsafe” non-EU products such as toys that violate the bloc’s rules arriving via Chinese e-commerce platforms.
“For years customs have been asked to take on illegal imports with limited resources while small parcels have multiplied out of control,” BEUC’s Agustin Reyna said.

The €2 handling fee is a permanent levy but the €3 duty on low-value packages is a temporary measure in place until July 1, 2028.

It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”
